task: Teaching a concept. A new teammate must change the code that handles incoming payment events, adding a new event type, and has never met the idea of idempotency. Facts: the system can deliver the same event twice; processing an event twice would charge a customer twice; the code prevents this by recording each event's unique id in the same database transaction as the charge, and skipping any id already recorded; a new event type must go through the same check, and must have an id that is the same every time that event is delivered. Write the message that teaches them the concept well enough to make the change safely.

properties.key:
A good message has these properties:
P1. The opening one or two sentences give the human what they most need from the message, before any background. Here: why the concept matters to their change.
P2. The term is defined in plain words.
P3. A concrete example from this system shows what goes wrong without it and how the code prevents it.
P4. It states what their change must keep: the same check, recorded with the charge, and an id that is the same on every delivery.
P5. It stands alone: every system-specific name the human needs is explained, general engineering terms may be assumed, and it relies on no earlier conversation.
P6. No sentence could be removed without losing something the reader needs to act or understand.
Core properties: P2, P3, P4.
Source of the properties: director goal: a context-limited human who may be cold (B38). The corpus has no teaching guidance today; these properties are the goal applied, and this is the probe most exposed to the author's preference.
properties.rubric: Judge only the message. 2 if every property holds. 1 if exactly one property fails and it is not a core property. 0 otherwise. In the reason, list the ID of every property that fails, or write 'all hold'.
